sections.heading: Let my whole life become prayer
sections.text: Great God, whether I am with your people or alone, at church or at home, let my life be soaked in prayer. Teach me to come to you again and again, not trusting my own words, but trusting the blood of Jesus that makes sinners welcome. Help me and protect me as long as I am still living here by faith, until the day prayer gives way to unhindered praise in your presence.
theological_themes: A life of continual prayer depends on grace, not performance.
Access to God is made possible through Christ's atoning blood.
Earthly prayer anticipates the unbroken worship of eternity.

scripture_references.connection: This passage grounds the believer's confidence to draw near to God in the blood of Jesus and his priestly work, which directly supports the prayer's dependence on atonement rather than personal worthiness.
The promise of a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy gives biblical language for prayer being stirred up by God's own gracious work, not merely by human effort.
The vision of God's servants worshiping him in the new creation illuminates the prayer's hope that present praying will one day become unbroken praise.

sections.heading: I come because I need you and because you invite me
sections.text: I come to you because I am needy, because your promises call me, and because your Spirit draws me. I do not want to treat your presence casually. You are holy, majestic, great, and glorious. Still, I do not run away from you, because your love gives me courage to come close.
theological_themes: God is approached with reverent fear because he is holy and glorious.
God's promises and the Spirit's work encourage believers to come near.
The Father's love gives confidence without removing reverence.

scripture_references.connection: Because Jesus is the great high priest, believers are invited to approach God's throne for mercy and help; this holds together deep need and real confidence.
Paul teaches that the Spirit enables believers to approach God as Father, which supports the prayer's movement from fear of God's greatness to courage in his love.
This text speaks of God as greatly feared and held in awe among his people, grounding the prayer's reverence before God's majesty.

sections.heading: I have nothing to pay, so I hold on to Jesus
sections.text: Before you, I am poor and guilty. I have nothing of my own that could repay you or balance what I owe. But by faith I hold on to Jesus. I place his righteousness where my sins stand against me. I have nothing to put on my side of the scale, but he is more than enough. His obedience, his blood, and his finished work satisfy your justice for me.
theological_themes: Human beings have no spiritual wealth with which to pay their debt before God.
Faith rests on Christ's righteousness rather than personal merit.
Christ's atonement satisfies divine justice for sinners.

scripture_references.connection: Paul rejects any righteousness of his own and wants to be found in Christ with the righteousness that comes through faith, which closely matches the prayer's plea to be represented by Christ's righteousness.
This passage explains that God justifies sinners through Christ's redemption and propitiation while remaining just, directly supporting the claim that Christ satisfies God's justice.
Paul describes the exchange in which Christ bears sin so that believers become righteous in him, illuminating the prayer's confidence that Jesus stands in the place of the guilty.

sections.heading: My sin is serious, but your mercy in Christ is deeper
sections.text: I praise you that my great sin has not exhausted your grace. I know even the sins I call small deserve your judgment, because they are sins against you, the infinite and holy God. But there is mercy for me in Christ. Where my guilt is most frightening, your mercy in him is free, deep, and stronger than my sin.
theological_themes: Sin is measured by the holiness of the God it offends.
Grace does not minimize guilt; it overcomes guilt in Christ.
God's mercy is especially displayed in forgiving serious sinners through Jesus.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, which directly supports the prayer's praise that great guilt draws out the greatness of grace in Christ.
David confesses that sin is ultimately against God, grounding the prayer's insistence that even sin people consider small is deeply serious because of who God is.
Paul presents himself as a great sinner who received mercy as a display of Christ's patience, supporting the prayer's confidence that terrible guilt does not put a sinner beyond mercy.

sections.heading: Show me more of Christ and speak peace to my heart
sections.text: Bless me by showing me more of the saving worth of Jesus. Let me see your goodness more clearly. Speak peace to my broken and repentant heart, not because I have made myself clean, but because Christ is enough for me.
theological_themes: Believers need God to reveal more of Christ's saving sufficiency.
God's goodness is known as he makes himself known to his people.
Peace with God comes through Christ, especially to the contrite who cast themselves on mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Moses asks to see God's glory, and God responds by proclaiming his goodness; this supports the prayer's request for God to make his goodness known.
Paul states that justification by faith brings peace with God through Jesus Christ, grounding the prayer's request for peace in Christ's sufficiency rather than self-improvement.
The psalm teaches that God does not despise a broken and contrite heart, which fits the prayer's plea for peace spoken to a repentant heart.

sections.heading: Do not let me stop seeking you until Christ rules all of me
sections.text: Keep me praying and refusing to let go until Christ rules every part of me—every thought, every word, every action. Give me the kind of faith that cleanses my heart, overcomes the pull of the world, shows itself in love, fastens me to you, and keeps me clinging to the cross.
theological_themes: The goal of prayer is not only pardon but Christ's practical rule in the whole life.
Saving faith purifies, perseveres, overcomes the world, and works through love.
Growth in holiness depends on continuing dependence on Christ and his cross.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers not to let sin reign but to present themselves to God under grace, supporting the prayer's longing for Christ to rule thought, speech, and conduct.
This verse describes faith working through love, which directly supports the prayer's desire for a living faith that expresses itself in love.
John says faith is the victory that overcomes the world, grounding the prayer's request for faith that resists the world's power.
The call to run with endurance while looking to Jesus supports the prayer's desire to keep clinging to Christ and persevering in holiness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original includes the strong Reformed claim that even the least sin deserves infinite punishment because it is committed against an infinite God. This is preserved in substance as a serious statement about sin deserving God's judgment, though phrased in more natural contemporary language.

The image of Christ's righteousness outweighing the believer's sin on the scales can sound transactional if isolated. The adaptation keeps the concrete image while anchoring it in Christ's righteousness, blood, and finished work satisfying divine justice.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Each prayer perfumed with the incense of atoning blood” was rendered as prayer being welcomed because of Jesus' blood, to preserve the mediation/atonement idea without retaining archaic devotional imagery.

“I bring Jesus to thee in the arms of faith” was interpreted as faith laying hold of Christ and pleading his righteousness, not as the believer offering Christ to God in an independent or meritorious way.

“Give thee no rest” was rendered as persistent prayer and refusal to let go, rather than irreverent pressure on God, because the original expresses persevering dependence until Christ reigns fully in the believer.
